definitions.meaning: a fine line of breeding in plants or animals, a good bloodline
rolling stock on a railway: a freight train made of wagons

explanation.surface: A farmer praises a fine line of livestock, perhaps one that rolls about.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as two words it is a quality bloodline; read as a phrase it is a freight train, the 'rolling' kind of stock in railway jargon.
explanation.definitionFit: A good strain is a fine breed; a goods train is railway rolling stock carrying freight.

definitions.meaning: a cinch, something handed over at no effort

explanation.definitionFit: A cinch is called a present in slang, and a natural flair is a present from nature, both senses of one word.

clue.text: Violent injury is not in vogue

parts.note: the opposite of in is out
something all the rage is in fashion, so rage means vogue

explanation.surface: A fashion writer declares that violent harm has gone out of style.
explanation.definitionFit: An atrocity or act of grave wrong done to someone is a synonym for a violent injury.

clue.text: Calling beyond compare, says the song

definitions.text: Calling beyond compare, says the song

parts.words: Calling beyond compare, says the song
parts.note: a calling is a profession; the Irving Berlin song claims there is no profession like this entertainment trade

explanation.surface: A singer proclaims that a certain vocation is unrivalled.
explanation.walkthrough: The song is Irving Berlin's 'There's No Business Like Show Business', so the profession it praises is beyond compare.
explanation.definitionFit: The entertainment industry is a calling, and the famous song says there is none like it.

clue.text: Passed right to the top, but fell back

indicators.note: in a down answer the top is the start, so the letter for right is placed before the other piece

parts.note: time that has passed has elapsed

explanation.surface: Someone recovering passed the right test to reach the top, then slid backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: To relapse is to slip back into a former state, such as illness, so it means fell back.

parts.note: something that lives exists, that is, it is
to sue is to plead or petition, as in suing for peace

explanation.surface: A lawyer's life consists of pleading for good outcomes.
explanation.definitionFit: Outcomes or consequences are what something issues in, so issues are results.

indicators.note: the letters are taken from inside the words a renegade

explanation.surface: A traitor lets slip a mild curse.
explanation.definitionFit: A softened form of 'by God', an old-fashioned exclamation, is a classic minced oath.

clue.text: Lady, old, and putting on weight all round

indicators.note: the unit of weight goes all round the other word, enclosing it

parts.note: a gram is a unit of weight
taken as written

explanation.surface: An elderly woman is getting heavier everywhere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'putting on' is only a link here, though it suggests gaining weight in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic word for a grandmother, or any old woman, fits an old lady.

clue.text: Habit holds listener in in gloom

indicators.note: the garment word holds the other pieces within it

parts.note: a habit is a garment, as worn by a nun, so dress
the ear is the organ that listens
taken as written

explanation.surface: A nun's habit keeps someone listening in, in a state of gloom.
explanation.definitionFit: Dullness and dismal bleakness make a near synonym for gloom.

indicators.note: something involved is tangled up, so the letters of these two words are mixed together

explanation.surface: A man named Thomas is so self-absorbed that he is dreadful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'self-involved' reads as one word for selfish, but 'self' is fodder and 'involved' the anagram signal on THOMAS plus SELF.
explanation.definitionFit: Abysmal literally means like an abyss, bottomless, too deep to be sounded.

definitions.meaning: a roller is a long breaking sea swell
to flap the hand back and forth in greeting

explanation.definitionFit: A swell on the sea is a roller, and to flutter or swing your hand is the other sense.

parts.note: something repeated happens a second time
a fiddle is a swindle or fraud

explanation.surface: A junior employee keeps committing the same fraud.
explanation.walkthrough: The violin sense of 'fiddle' is hidden behind the swindle sense; playing the lesser violin part is the idiom.
explanation.definitionFit: To play the lesser part is to be in a subordinate, junior position.

indicators.note: the word for call goes about the letter, surrounding it

parts.note: to dub is to call or name

explanation.surface: Someone telephones regarding a slur on their name.
explanation.definitionFit: To smear paint crudely is to plaster it on, so the words are synonyms.

clue.text: One who aspires to be a phoney ?

definitions.meaning: a claimant to a throne aspires to it, like the Old and Young claimants of the Stuart line
someone who only feigns, a fake

explanation.definitionFit: A claimant to a title aspires to it, and someone who feigns is a fake: two senses of the same word.

parts.note: potent means strong

indicators.note: tea that is brewed is stewed and stirred, so the letters of teas are mixed up

explanation.surface: Strong tea is made for Indian princes.
explanation.definitionFit: Rajahs are Indian princes and rulers, examples of mighty monarchs.

clue.text: A maiden often embraces Gaelic superintendent

indicators.note: the cricket term embraces, wrapping round, the language

parts.note: in cricket a maiden is an over in which no runs are scored
Erse is an old name for the Gaelic language

explanation.surface: A young woman often hugs her Irish-speaking supervisor.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket an over is six balls bowled by one player; a maiden is one with no runs scored, so a maiden is an over.
explanation.definitionFit: A supervisor or foreman in charge of workers is a superintendent.

parts.note: a man from the year of the Battle of Hastings, one of the conquering invaders from northern France

explanation.walkthrough: 1066 is the year of the Conquest of England by William of Normandy; the question mark admits that the answer is also a man's name.
explanation.definitionFit: The invaders of 1066 came from a duchy in northern France, and the word is also a common forename for a chap.

parts.note: port is a fortified wine, a drink
rays are beams of light

explanation.surface: Someone takes a drink and smiles broadly.
explanation.definitionFit: To depict in a picture or in words is to draw.

parts.note: echoes Francis Bacon's 'Reading maketh a full man', but read literally the activity that fills a man up

explanation.walkthrough: Bacon's essay says reading makes a full (well-stocked) man; the literal-minded take is the act of consuming food.
explanation.definitionFit: Consuming food is what literally fills a man's stomach.

indicators.note: the compass points go in the word for characteristic

parts.note: a trait is a characteristic
N and S, two points of the compass

explanation.surface: Two marks fall inside a typical stretch of text.
explanation.definitionFit: Passage means travel through or across somewhere, as in goods in transport.

parts.note: cordial means warm and friendly

explanation.surface: An amiable son buys a round of drinks.
explanation.definitionFit: Cordials are sweet fruit syrups or liqueurs, kinds of beverage.

clue.text: Constitutional examiner and recorder, we hear

indicators.note: the clue tells us the recorder's title is only heard, so the spelling changes

parts.note: an annalist records events year by year

explanation.surface: A specialist in the constitution also keeps records, apparently.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'constitution' is the make-up of a substance, which a chemist breaks down into components.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who breaks down a substance's make-up into its components examines its constitution.

clue.text: Look to be in grim distress

indicators.note: the word for look is put in the word for grim

parts.note: dour means grim or stern
lo is an old word meaning look

explanation.surface: Someone seems to be in dreadful trouble.
explanation.definitionFit: Dolour is a literary word for sorrow or grief, deep distress.

definitions.meaning: rapture, as in being carried away with joy
a vehicle or means of conveyance that moves people or goods

explanation.definitionFit: A rapture carries you away, and a bus or ship carries people: both senses of carrying across.

parts.note: I is one form of 'the' in Italian, the masculine plural article
ran means fled

explanation.surface: An Italian man fled his homeland.
explanation.definitionFit: Iran is a nation in the Middle East, an example of a country.

clue.text: What is good when there isn't any

definitions.text: What is good when there isn't any

parts.words: What is good when there isn't any
parts.note: plays on the saying that no tidings are good tidings

explanation.surface: A riddle about something that is welcome only in its absence.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb is 'No news is good news'.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb says the absence of tidings is a good sign.

definitions.meaning: to try something out, to trial it
a standard against which something is judged

explanation.definitionFit: To try is to trial or examine, and a criterion is a standard or yardstick, both senses of one word.

clue.text: He tried unsuccessfully to kill Holmes

definitions.text: He tried unsuccessfully to kill Holmes

parts.words: He tried unsuccessfully to kill Holmes
parts.note: the creator of the detective sent him over the Reichenbach Falls but public demand forced his return

explanation.surface: A would-be murderer fails to dispose of a famous detective.
explanation.walkthrough: The author killed Sherlock Holmes in 'The Final Problem' (1893), then revived him after readers protested.
explanation.definitionFit: The Scottish author created Sherlock Holmes, then tried to end the series by killing him off.

definitions.meaning: to put down or position things
Wimbledon is the London tennis championship, whose matches are divided into these scoring units

explanation.definitionFit: To put down is to place, and tennis matches at Wimbledon, the London championship, are played in units of games.

indicators.note: the word for expectations goes about the letter, surrounding it

parts.note: prospects are expectations for the future
U means upper-class, as in Nancy Mitford's U and non-U

explanation.surface: A school's informant has hopes about posh pupils.
explanation.walkthrough: U for upper-class is a British convention, from Nancy Mitford's U and non-U usage.
explanation.definitionFit: A brochure that tells parents about a school's courses and character informs them.
